lessons.title: Determinants, eigenvalues and eigenvectors: what a matrix does to its own directions
covers_outcomes: Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a small matrix by hand and verify the result by substitution.
Explain what the determinant says about invertibility and volume scaling, including its sign.
Determine whether a matrix is diagonalisable and explain what failure to be diagonalisable means.

numbered_objects: Theorem 4.12 (eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent)

prerequisites.need: Linear independence. The test for a nonzero solution of (A - λI)v = 0 is a statement about dependence of the columns.
Matrices as linear mappings. Without the mapping reading, 'the direction it does not rotate' is not a meaningful question.
Solvability of systems. You need the fact that a square homogeneous system has a nonzero solution exactly when its matrix is singular.

provenance.source_supported: The determinant as a volume-scaling and orientation factor, the characteristic polynomial, algebraic multiplicity, eigenspaces, the independence of eigenvectors with distinct eigenvalues, and the spectral theorem are all taken from MML sections 4.1 and 4.2, with the printed pages recorded above.
provenance.established_theory: The derivation of the 2x2 determinant from the area of the image parallelogram, the trace and determinant invariants proved from the characteristic polynomial, the diagonalisation argument for repeated application, and the counterexamples in the misconception section are standard results written out here in full.
provenance.original_examples: Every numerical instance used for teaching (the matrix [[2,1],[1,2]], the defective matrix [[1,1],[0,1]], the non-defective repeated-eigenvalue matrix, the exercise matrices, and all code) was chosen for this lesson. The book's own examples were not copied, and the book's figures are cited by number and page rather than reproduced.
provenance.not_covered_here: Computation of the determinant of large matrices, numerical conditioning of eigenproblems (MATH-19), and the eigendecomposition as a tool (MATH-07, next lesson). The Cholesky decomposition (MML 4.3) is deliberately skipped here.

lessons.title: Matrix decompositions: Cholesky, eigendecomposition, and the SVD that works for every matrix
covers_outcomes: State the existence conditions of the Cholesky, eigendecomposition and SVD, and give an example that violates each condition.
Use the SVD to describe the action of a matrix as rotation, scaling and rotation.
Relate the eigendecomposition of a symmetric positive-definite matrix to its Cholesky factor.

numbered_objects: Theorem 4.21 (a symmetric matrix can always be diagonalized)
Theorem 4.24 (the spectral norm of A is its largest singular value)

prerequisites.need: Eigenvalues, eigenspaces and the spectral theorem. The SVD is constructed from the eigendecomposition of A'A, so the whole derivation rests on the symmetric case.
Inner products, orthogonality and orthonormal bases. Without them 'orthogonal matrices' and 'the columns of U are orthonormal' carry no meaning.
Matrices as linear mappings, for the interpretation of the SVD as basis change, scaling and basis change.

provenance.source_supported: The Cholesky decomposition and its existence for symmetric positive-definite matrices (Theorem 4.18), the eigendecomposition and its existence conditions (Theorems 4.20, 4.21, Definition 4.19), the SVD theorem for any rectangular matrix (Theorem 4.22), the spectral norm as the largest singular value (Theorem 4.24) and the matrix phylogeny of section 4.7 are all taken from MML sections 4.3 to 4.7, with printed pages recorded above.
provenance.established_theory: The constructive proof of the SVD from the eigendecomposition of A'A, the induction proving existence of the Cholesky factorisation, the uniqueness argument for the Cholesky factor, the fast powers-of-sigma bound used to derive the spectral norm, and the worked examples are standard results written out in full here. Where the source leaves a proof to the reader or states a result without proof, the lesson says so rather than presenting the gap as covered.
provenance.original_examples: Every numerical instance (the 2x2 SPD matrix, the rectangular 3x2 matrix, the non-diagonalisable counterexample, the badly conditioned matrix in the code section, and all code) was produced for this lesson. The source's Figure 4.8 is cited by number and not reproduced, and the book's movie-ratings example is not reused.
provenance.not_covered_here: Numerical computation of the SVD (Golub-Kahan bidiagonalisation), the cost and conditioning of each decomposition (MATH-19, no source in the repository), and the low-rank approximation theorem, which is the subject of LSN-MATH-08-01.

lessons.title: Low-rank approximation: what to throw away, and what it costs
covers_outcomes: Derive the best rank-k approximation in the Frobenius norm from the SVD and state the size of the error.
Apply rank truncation to a data matrix and interpret the retained components.
Explain the trade-off between representation size and reconstruction error.

numbered_objects: equation 4.90 (A as a sum of rank-1 matrices u_i v_i^T)
Theorem 4.24 (the spectral norm of A is its largest singular value)
Figure 4.11 (outer products of an image, cited not reproduced)

prerequisites.need: The SVD, its outer-product form A = sum sigma_i u_i v_i^T, and the identity ||A||_2 = sigma_1. The truncation is defined by the first of these and its error is measured by the second.
Orthogonality and the norm identities, so that 'the best approximation in a norm' has a meaning you can compute with.

interactive.serves: The size-error trade-off is a curve, not a fact. The demonstration lets the reader move along it and watch which structure in the matrix survives.

provenance.source_supported: The matrix as a sum of rank-1 outer products (MML equation 4.90), the Eckart-Young theorem for the spectral norm with equations 4.94 and 4.95, and the connection to eigenvector computation and low-rank approximations in PCA (MML section 10.4) are taken from the source, with printed pages recorded above.
provenance.established_theory: The optimality proof for the spectral norm is written out in full here, including the interlacing step. The Frobenius-norm version of optimality is stated as a theorem with its source recorded, and the achievement half (the exact error of the truncated SVD) is proved here. The storage arithmetic, the energy criterion and the numerical-rank discussion are engineering consequences worked out here.
provenance.source_gap: The supplied text states Theorem 4.25 for the spectral norm only, and the word 'Frobenius' does not occur anywhere in the supplied markdown. MATH-08's second outcome asks for the Frobenius-norm result, so that half of the competency is recorded as partly sourced in the coverage report, with a supplemental source required. The lesson says which parts are sourced and which are not, rather than blurring them.
provenance.original_examples: The matrix used for teaching is synthetic and generated by tools/build_demo_data.py from three explicit formulas, stated in the lesson. The book's image example (Figure 4.11) is cited by number and size but not reproduced, and no real dataset is claimed.
provenance.not_covered_here: Numerical rank thresholds in practice, randomised low-rank approximation for very large matrices, and the cost of computing an SVD at scale. These are recorded gaps (MATH-19).

exercises.prompt: For B = [[2, 0, 3], [1, 4, -1], [0, 2, 1]], compute the determinant twice: by Sarrus' rule and by Laplace expansion along the first row. Confirm that the two agree, and state whether B is invertible.
exercises.expected_outcome: Correct determinant by two independent expansions, and the conclusion det B != 0 so B is invertible.
exercises.solution_verified_by: independent symbolic computation with sympy (tools/run_content_checks.py, check math06_ex01_determinant)

exercises.prompt: Explain, without a full expansion, why det([[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[1,2,3]]) = 0, and name the property of the determinant you used. Then construct a 4x4 matrix whose determinant is 0 for a different reason.
exercises.expected_outcome: Identification of the alternating (or multilinearity) property when two rows coincide, plus a second, structurally different reason for a zero determinant.
exercises.solution_verified_by: independent symbolic computation with sympy and manual reasoning recorded in the solution

origin_detail.section: 4.3 exercises (printed p.139), exercise 4.3 in the source's numbering asks the same question for two 2x2 matrices
origin_detail.note: The task is the source's; the matrices are ours, so that the book's own exercise remains unsolved here for independent practice.

exercises.prompt: Compute all eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenspaces of A = [[3,1],[1,3]] and of C = [[2,2],[1,3]] by hand. Verify each eigenpair by substitution, and verify both eigenvalues against the trace and the determinant.
exercises.expected_outcome: Four correct eigenpairs with eigenspaces given as spans, each verified by substitution and by the trace/determinant invariants.
exercises.solution_verified_by: independent symbolic computation with sympy (check math06_ex03_eigenpairs)

origin_detail.section: 4.5 exercises (printed p.138), exercise 4.5 in the source's numbering uses four matrices for the same question
origin_detail.note: The question is the source's (diagonalisability is unrelated to invertibility); the five matrices are ours.

exercises.prompt: Complete a 5x2 table for the matrices listed in the solution file: for each, decide whether it is invertible and whether it is diagonalisable over R, and give the reason for each answer. Two of the five require the same matrix to be invertible but not diagonalisable over R.
exercises.expected_outcome: Correct invertibility from the determinant, correct diagonalisability from the algebraic-versus-geometric multiplicity comparison, and reasons that name the multiplicities rather than the eigenvalues alone.
exercises.solution_verified_by: independent computation of multiplicities with numpy/sympy and manual reasoning recorded in the solution

exercises.prompt: Prove that if v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ, then v is an eigenvector of A^k with eigenvalue λ^k for every k >= 1. Then show that the converse fails: give a real 2x2 matrix A for which A^2 has a real eigenvalue that is not the square of any real eigenvalue of A.
exercises.expected_outcome: A correct induction argument, and a counterexample (a rotation matrix) together with the explanation that its eigenvalues are complex, which is what makes the real converse fail.
exercises.solution_verified_by: symbolic verification of the counterexample in sympy (check math06_ex05_converse)

exercises.prompt: Show that every real 3x3 matrix has at least one real eigenvalue, and give an example of a real 3x3 matrix with exactly one. Explain how this argument changes in dimension 2.
exercises.expected_outcome: The odd-degree real polynomial argument, a valid example (a rotation in a plane plus a scaling along the third axis), and the correct statement that the argument fails in even dimension with the rotation in 2D as the witness.
exercises.solution_verified_by: symbolic computation of the characteristic polynomials (check math06_ex06_odd_degree)

exercises.prompt: Implement a function eigen_2x2(A) that returns the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a real 2x2 matrix using the quadratic formula rather than a library decomposition. Test it against numpy.linalg.eig on 1000 random matrices and report the maximum residual ||A v - λ v||. Explain which matrices make the residual large and why the comparison is being made against a library at all.
exercises.expected_outcome: A working implementation, a measured residual, an identification of the ill-conditioned cases (nearly repeated eigenvalues), and a statement of what the test does and does not establish.
exercises.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the implementation handles both real and complex eigenvalue cases rather than ignoring one; (2) the residual is measured rather than asserted; (3) at least one concrete example of a matrix where the two disagree is shown, with the reason; (4) the answer states that agreement with numpy establishes consistency, not correctness, unless the mathematics is checked independently too.
exercises.solution_verified_by: the reference implementation was executed by check_ex07_reference_implementation; the reported residuals and the near-defective case are its recorded output

exercises.prompt: Compute the Cholesky factor of A = [[9, 6, 3], [6, 5, 2], [3, 2, 2]] by hand using the column formulas, verify LL' = A, and explain which of the three diagonal entries of L would be imaginary if a single entry of A were changed, and why the factorisation would then not exist over the reals.
exercises.expected_outcome: A correct lower-triangular L with positive diagonal, an exact verification of LL' = A, and an explanation that the third pivot is the Schur complement whose positivity is exactly the positive-definiteness condition.
exercises.solution_verified_by: independent Cholesky computation with numpy.linalg.cholesky and exact symbolic verification of LL' = A

origin_detail.section: Chapter 4 exercises 4.8 and 4.9 (printed p.138): 'Find the SVD of the matrix' / 'Find the singular value decomposition of'
origin_detail.note: The task is the source's, which asks for the full SVD of a given matrix; the matrix here is a 3x2 rectangle chosen by this lesson so that U must be completed with a third orthogonal direction, a step the source's own matrices do not force.

exercises.prompt: Compute the full SVD of A = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1]]. Work through the construction: form A'A, find its eigenvalues and an orthonormal eigenbasis, obtain the singular values and the right-singular vectors, then compute u_i = Av_i/sigma_i and extend the set to an orthonormal basis of the left space. Verify A = U Sigma V' by multiplying out, and state which singular values are zero and why.
exercises.expected_outcome: sigma = (sqrt(3), 1), an explicit U (3x3, including the direction orthogonal to the columns of A), Sigma 3x2, V 2x2, a verified reconstruction, and the observation that no singular value is zero because the columns of A are independent.
exercises.solution_verified_by: exact symbolic reconstruction with sympy and comparison against numpy.linalg.svd

exercises.prompt: For each of the three decompositions in this lesson, give a matrix that violates its existence condition, with a one-line reason: a symmetric matrix with no Cholesky factor, a square matrix with no eigendecomposition, and — if you can — a matrix with no SVD. Then verify each failure numerically and explain what the failing computation actually does.
exercises.expected_outcome: A valid non-positive-definite symmetric matrix, a defective square matrix, the correct statement that no matrix lacks an SVD, and observations about what the library routines return or raise in the failing cases.
exercises.solution_verified_by: the failures were executed and their outcomes recorded (numpy raises LinAlgError for the Cholesky failure; eig returns fewer independent eigenvectors)

exercises.prompt: Prove that ||A||_F^2 equals the sum of the squared singular values of A, and that ||A x|| <= sigma_1 ||x|| for every x. Use the SVD, not the entries. Then explain in one sentence why the second result is the reason sigma_1 is called the spectral norm.
exercises.expected_outcome: Both derivations from the SVD expansion of A, correct handling of the orthogonality of U and V, and the identification of sigma_1 as the operator norm.
exercises.solution_verified_by: both identities checked numerically on 200 random matrices, recording the maximum deviation

exercises.prompt: A'A and AA' have the same nonzero eigenvalues (Chapter 4 exercise 4.11, printed p.138, which you should do separately). Instead, explain why their zero eigenvalues can differ in multiplicity: give a rectangular example where one of the two matrices is singular with a large null space and the other is not singular at all, and connect the null space of A'A to the null space of A.
exercises.expected_outcome: A correct example (for instance a short-and-wide or tall-and-narrow full-rank matrix), the identity ker(A'A) = ker(A) proved in a line, and the resulting multiplicities counted.
exercises.solution_verified_by: null spaces and eigenvalue counts computed symbolically for the example

exercises.prompt: Take an SPD matrix and compare two different square roots of it: the triangular Cholesky factor L and the symmetric square root A^{1/2} = Q Lambda^{1/2} Q'. Show both satisfy SS' = A, show they are different, and characterise every square root of A as Q Lambda^{1/2} W' for an orthogonal W. Then say which square root a sampling routine should use if it wants x = A^{1/2} z to have covariance A with the fewest operations, and why.
exercises.expected_outcome: Both factors verified, the general form proved from the spectral decomposition, and the correct practical answer with a reason (the triangular factor is cheaper for a single solve, and its structure is what makes the sampling transform cheap).
exercises.solution_verified_by: both square roots computed exactly, the orthogonal W extracted from the relation and verified to be orthogonal, and both products confirmed to equal A

exercises.prompt: Implement the textbook construction of the SVD: eigen-decompose A'A, take square roots of the eigenvalues, and build U from Av_i/sigma_i. Compare with numpy's SVD on 100 random matrices, then on matrices whose singular values span a wide range (epsilon chosen so that the ratio is around 1e8). Report at which ratio the construction stops delivering accurate small singular values, and explain why forming A'A is the cause.
exercises.expected_outcome: A working implementation, measured agreement on well-conditioned inputs, a measured loss of accuracy on ill-conditioned ones, and the explanation that forming A'A squares the ratio of largest to smallest singular value, which is exactly the information the small singular values carry.
exercises.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) the implementation handles rectangular matrices, not only square ones; (2) the comparison is quantitative (relative error in each singular value, not just 'it matched'); (3) the ill-conditioned experiment is run with a stated epsilon and the resulting error is reported; (4) the answer states clearly that numpy does not use this construction, so agreement tells you the mathematics is right, not that the algorithm is good.
exercises.solution_verified_by: the reference implementation was executed and its measured relative errors are the recorded output of check_ex07_gram_svd_accuracy

origin_detail.section: Chapter 4 exercise 4.10 (printed p.138): 'Find the rank-1 approximation of' a given matrix
origin_detail.note: The task is the source's; the matrix is different, so the source's own matrix remains unsolved for independent practice.

exercises.prompt: Find the best rank-1 approximation of A = [[3, 0], [4, 5]] by hand: compute the SVD, form sigma_1 u_1 v_1', and state the exact Frobenius and spectral norms of the residual. Then confirm that the singular values you found are consistent with det A and the trace of A'A.
exercises.expected_outcome: sigma = (3*sqrt(5), sqrt(5)), the rank-1 term equal to (3/2)[[1,1],[3,3]], a residual whose spectral norm is sqrt(5) and whose squared Frobenius norm is 5.
exercises.solution_verified_by: exact symbolic computation of the SVD, the rank-1 term, and both residual norms

exercises.prompt: Write out the proof that no matrix of rank at most k can approximate A better than the truncated SVD in the spectral norm. The key step is a dimension argument: intersect the null space of the candidate with the span of the first k+1 right-singular vectors, and bound the norm of A on that intersection.
exercises.expected_outcome: A complete proof: the intersection is non-trivial by dimension count, a unit vector in it satisfies ||Ax|| >= sigma_{k+1}, and the candidate annihilates it, so ||A - B||_2 >= sigma_{k+1}.
exercises.solution_verified_by: the dimension count and the inequality were checked symbolically on random rectangular matrices, and the bound was tested against random rank-k candidates

exercises.prompt: Using the recorded SVD in content/demos/rank-truncation.json, reconstruct the matrix at k = 1, 3, 8 and 12. Report the relative Frobenius error and the retained energy at each, and verify that the recorded values in the file match the theorem's prediction sum_{i>k} sigma_i^2.
exercises.expected_outcome: Correct reconstructions, correct identification of the cumulative-energy relation, and the observation that the relative error is the square root of the discarded energy fraction.
exercises.solution_verified_by: the reconstruction and both error measures were computed and compared with the values recorded in the demo file

exercises.prompt: Derive the storage break-even rule for a rank-k factorisation of an m x n matrix: k(m + n + 1) < mn. Then compute the largest k that compresses a 1432 x 1910 image (the size of the matrix the source uses in its Figure 4.11 discussion) and the storage ratio for k = 50 and k = 200.
exercises.expected_outcome: The rearranged inequality k < mn/(m+n+1), the largest integer k = 818 for that size, and the two ratios, with the observation that the rule is an upper bound that ignores metadata.
exercises.solution_verified_by: the arithmetic was computed exactly and the rule verified against the recorded storage table in the demo file

exercises.prompt: Construct a 6x6 matrix whose singular values decay to 1e-14, and show that its numerical rank depends on the threshold: report the rank at thresholds 1e-3, 1e-8 and 1e-12 relative to sigma_1. Then write one paragraph on what a 'rank-deficient' matrix means when the singular values are tiny rather than zero, and why the truncation is still the right thing to do.
exercises.expected_outcome: A constructed matrix, three different reported ranks for the same matrix, and an explanation that the rank decision is a modelling choice justified by the error it induces, not a property read off the matrix.
exercises.solution_verified_by: the ranks at each threshold were computed and the induced reconstruction errors reported

exercises.prompt: Take the demo matrix and choose k by two different criteria: (a) the smallest k that retains 99% of the energy, and (b) the smallest k that keeps the relative Frobenius error below 1%. Report both values, both errors, and both storage ratios. Then argue which criterion you would use for a downstream linear model, and state explicitly what neither criterion captures.
exercises.expected_outcome: Two different k values with their measured errors and costs, and an argument that goes beyond 'smaller error is better' — for instance that neither criterion knows anything about the downstream task or about noise in the small components.
exercises.rubric: Full credit requires: (1) both k values computed rather than estimated; (2) the errors and storage ratios reported as numbers; (3) an argument that names at least one thing the energy criterion ignores, such as the possibility that a discarded component carries signal; (4) no claim that either criterion is optimal.
exercises.solution_verified_by: both criteria were evaluated on the recorded SVD and their k values, errors and costs are the recorded output of check_ex06_selection_criteria
